I will keep my land in the cropping pattern I trust most here in southern Hebei: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I know this system, I have the machinery and work rhythm for it, and it fits Quzhou County better than taking a big risk on a new cash crop. At my age, I would rather aim for stable output and manageable fieldwork than chase a higher but less certain return. Wheat gives me a dependable first harvest, and maize makes full use of the summer heat and rain after wheat comes off.

For wheat, I will stay with an improved variety instead of old saved seed, because I want better uniformity, lodging resistance, and yield stability, but I do not want an expensive or complicated package. I will fertilize in a moderate way, not too heavy on nitrogen, because too much pushes weak growth and raises disease risk. I will use rotary tillage because it is practical for me and matches the equipment I can get easily. I will irrigate only at the key times, because water matters here and I do not want waste. I will spray only when needed for the main diseases and insects, keeping it controlled rather than excessive.

After wheat harvest, I will go straight into summer maize on the same land. I will use hybrid maize because the yield is steadier and the plants are stronger, which matters in a hot summer with uneven rainfall. I will cut tillage and use no-tillage for maize after wheat if field conditions allow, because that saves time, keeps moisture, and reduces labor at the busiest moment of the year. I will give maize enough nitrogen to support grain filling, with balanced phosphorus and potassium underneath. Irrigation will stay limited, because summer rain usually does part of the work, and I only want to step in when the crop truly needs it. Overall, I am choosing the plan that is most familiar, most workable, and most likely to give me a reliable year.
